name: Sulod
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Only Jocano 1968 (ethnography). Zorc 1977 (PL C-44, read) lists Sulud as West Bisayan but gives no Sulod-specific accent data.

new_statements.citation: one of the works listed for this language (see the verification note)
new_statements.check: reported on verification, not yet confirmed
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work is listed for sulo1237 and the compiler opened it, so there were no silent/unopened listed works to spot-check. As a substitute I a full-text search for stress/accent the other texts already saved in the same folder (not listed works, not added): p.248 'Stress patterns are overwhelmingly similar especially among cognates' (Panay West Bisayan varieties in general, no Sulod data point); line 291 'accent (length or stress) patterns were ignored' (methodological note for the lexicostatistics, no Sulod accent statement); jocano_hinilawod_tarangban1_intro scanned: no stress/accent hits. Nothing missed that bears on Sulod stress placement.

sources.citation: Zorc, R. David. 1977. The Bisayan dialects of the Philippines: subgrouping and reconstruction. Pacific Linguistics C-44. Canberra: ANU.
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL5629 .Z6
sources.note: Table 2 no.19 lists 'Sulud' only as an alternate name for Kinaray-a (WBs); accent sections (3.1.3, 8.10) give no Sulod-specific data.

sources.citation: SEAlang Library, R. David Zorc field-notes archive (envelope menu).
sources.note: No Sulod envelope exists (Panay envelopes: Kinaray-a, Pandan, Capiznon, Hiligaynon, Aklanon).

sources.citation: Rentillo, Philip. 2025. Lexicophonetic dialectology of Panay. Dialectologia 34: 235-271. doi:10.1344/dialectologia.34.10
sources.note: No Sulod data. Sec. 1.2.5 p.241: 'The much less studied Sulod or Suludnon (ISO 639-3 srg).. Its speakers settle mostly in very remote and rugged areas.. which is why formal dialectological studies are technically non-existent.' p.248 (Panay varieties sampled, Sulod not among them): 'Stress patterns are overwhelmingly similar especially among cognates.'

sources.citation: Lobel, Jason W. 2013. Philippine and North Bornean languages: issues in description, subgrouping, and reconstruction. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa.
sources.note: Nothing on Sulod stress; fn.5 p.39: 'Panayan Binukidnon (sometimes referred to as "Sulod") is a Western Bisayan language closely related to the other languages surrounding it on Panay.'

sources.citation: Jocano, F. Landa. [2000]. Hinilawod: Adventures of Humadapnon, Tarangban I (Epic of Central Panay 2). Chanted by Hugan-an; recorded and translated by F. Landa Jocano. Metro Manila: PUNLAD Research House. (scan of pp. 1-88)
sources.note: Nothing. Only linguistic remark is the Note on p.8: 'Sulod language has not yet been phonemicized. The transcription used here for native terms is like the Philippine national language orthography except for the additional vowel /ə/.. A tentative phonemic analysis of Sulod language indicates the following segmental phonemes: /i a u ə p t k ʔ b d g m n ŋ l r s h y w/.' Epic text (pp.9-88) is printed without accent marks.

sources.citation: Zorc, R. David. 1972. The Western subgroup of Bisayan. Oceanic Linguistics 11(2): 110-139.
sources.note: No Sulod statement. fn.4 subgrouping: 'KINARAYAN: Kinaray-a (= Hinaray-a, Sulod, Antiqueño), Pandan.' Method note: 'different accent (length or stress) patterns were ignored' in the lexicostatistical scoring.
